messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Civil Servant
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss of Control: Lack of control, Sleeping Alone: Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Vignette:
Martin is a 54-year-old white American man who works as a civil servant in a county licensing office, where most of his days are structured around forms, procedures, and small interactions across a public counter. He came to treatment after months of telling himself he should be able to handle things on his own. What finally unsettled him was how much of his life had narrowed around one private rule: he could not bear to be alone. He is currently in a relationship and described his partner as kind and steady, but he also admitted, with embarrassment, that on nights when she was away he would go to considerable lengths not to sleep by himself. He would stay late with coworkers, linger at a neighbor’s house, or find some reason to be in a place where other people were nearby, because the prospect of lying alone in bed felt intolerable.

The abuse had occurred in a previous romantic relationship. Martin described episodes in which his partner became physically violent during arguments, especially at moments when he tried to leave the room, calm things down, or set a limit. What has stayed with him is not a single blow but the felt certainty of being trapped with someone stronger, angrier, and in command of what happened next. In recounting it, he circled repeatedly around the moment he realized he had no control over whether the assault would stop. Even now, that sense of helplessness is what he finds hardest to bear. Situations that leave him feeling constrained, overpowered, or unable to direct what happens around him can suddenly make his body feel as if he is back there, even when he knows where he is.

In the weeks after the relationship ended, Martin expected the memories to fade if he kept moving. Instead, he found that when they came, they did not feel like ordinary remembering. He said it was “like still shots,” as if photographs had been dropped into his mind: a particular angle of the room, the look on his partner’s face, the position of his own hands. Sometimes the memory returned with a sensory force that caught him off guard, including the taste in his mouth from the assault, vivid enough that he would stop what he was doing and swallow hard as though it were happening again. Yet when he tried on purpose to think through exactly what had happened, to tell himself the whole story in order, he found the memory strangely difficult to access. He could retrieve sharp fragments, but not a steady, deliberate account. That gap frustrated him and made him feel unsteady in his own mind.

Rather than dwell on any of it, Martin learned to push himself away from the memories whenever they surfaced. He described mentally stepping back from them, going numb and detached until the images dulled. He also began arranging his life so that he was almost never by himself. If he had no plans after work, he made some. At the office he stayed in the break room longer than he used to, volunteered to help others with end-of-day tasks, and timed his departure so he could walk out with someone rather than cross the nearly empty municipal building alone. It was not just silence he avoided. Being alone in a room or building made him feel exposed, as if there would be no witness and no way to regain control if something happened. Sleeping alone was worst of all. Hotel rooms during required work travel became ordeals, and unfamiliar places felt especially threatening once the door shut and he was left with his own thoughts.

One consequence has been a marked change in how he moves through his workplace and social life. Martin now keeps himself constantly surrounded by people, not because he is relaxed in company, but because company protects him from being left with his mind. This has made him seem more sociable on the surface, but he said it is exhausting and leaves little room for rest. Another painful complication is his discomfort being alone with men. In his job, male colleagues sometimes ask him to review paperwork in a side office or stay behind after a meeting, and he notices himself hesitating, scanning for an open door, or finding a reason to keep the interaction in a more public space. He feels ashamed of this, especially because he sees himself as practical and fair-minded, yet the unease is immediate and difficult to dismiss.

By the time he sought help, Martin was tired of organizing every day around avoiding isolation. He said he wants to be able to spend a night by himself without panic, to travel for work without dreading the hotel room, and to stop feeling overtaken by flashes that arrive with the force of photographs and taste. What frightens him most is the possibility that this constricted way of living will become permanent, that he will continue needing other people around not out of enjoyment but out of fear of what will happen if he is left alone with what he remembers.
